'''''Calocedrus decurrens''''', with the common names '''incense cedar'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=CADE27|taxon=Calocedrus decurrens|access-date=10 January 2016}}</ref> and  '''California incense cedar'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> (syn. ''Libocedrus decurrens'' Torr.), is a [[species]] of [[conifer]]ous tree in the cypress family, [[Cupressaceae]], native to western North America. It is the most widely known species in the genus, and is often simply called incense cedar without the regional qualifier.<ref name=fna>{{eFloras|1|233500299|Calocedrus decurrens|first=John W. |last=Thieret |family=Cupressaceae}}</ref><ref name=usfs>{{Silvics |volume=1 |genus=Libocedrus |species=decurrens |first1=Robert F. |last1=Powers |first2=William W. |last2=Oliver}}</ref><ref name=farjon>Farjon, A. (2005). ''Monograph of Cupressaceae and Sciadopitys''. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. {{ISBN|1-84246-068-4}}</ref>
{{toclimit|3}}

==Description==
''Calocedrus decurrens'' is a large tree, typically reaching heights of {{convert|30-40|m|round=5|sp=us}} and a trunk diameter up to {{convert|1.2|m|ftin|abbr=on}}. The largest known tree, located in [[Klamath National Forest]], [[Siskiyou County, California]], is {{convert|47.98|m|ftin|abbr=on}} tall with a {{convert|12|m|ftin|adj=on|abbr=on}} circumference trunk and a {{convert|17.5|m|adj=on|sigfig=3|frac=4|abbr=on}} spread.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date= |title=Incensecedar (Calocedrus decurrens) |url=https://www.americanforests.org/big-trees/incensecedar-calocedrus-decurrens/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170107081650/https://www.americanforests.org/big-trees/incensecedar-calocedrus-decurrens/ |archive-date=2017-01-07 |access-date=2022-03-11 |website=American Forests |language=en-US}}</ref> Specimens form a broad conic crown of spreading branches. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is orange-brown weathering grayish, smooth at first, becoming fissured and exfoliating in long strips on the lower trunk on old trees.<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last1=Arno |first1=Stephen F. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qDD4DwAAQBAJ |title=Northwest Trees: Identifying & Understanding the Region's Native Trees |last2=Hammerly |first2=Ramona P. |publisher=[[Mountaineers Books]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-1-68051-329-5 |edition=field guide |location=Seattle |pages=149–155 |language=en |oclc=1141235469 |orig-date=1977}}</ref> Specimens can live to over 500 years old.<ref name=":02" />

The foliage is produced in flattened sprays with scale-like [[leaves]] {{convert|2–15|mm|in|frac=32|abbr=on}} long; they are arranged in opposite [[decussate]] pairs, with the successive pairs closely then distantly spaced, so forming apparent whorls of four; the facial pairs are flat, with the lateral pairs folded over their bases. The leaves are bright green on both sides of the shoots, with only inconspicuous [[stoma]]ta.<ref name="farjon" /> The foliage, when crushed, gives off an aroma somewhat akin to shoe-polish.

The [[seed cones]] are {{convert|20–35|mm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} long, pale green to yellow, with four (rarely six) scales arranged in opposite decussate pairs; the outer pair of scales each bears two winged [[seed]]s, the inner pair(s) usually being sterile and fused together in a flat plate. The cones turn orange to yellow-brown when mature about 8 months after pollination. The pollen cones are {{convert|6–8|mm|in|frac=32|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="farjon" />

==Distribution==
The bulk of the tree's range is in the United States, from central-southwestern [[Oregon]] through most of [[California]]<ref name=":02" /> and the extreme west of [[Nevada]], as well as a short distance into northwest Mexico in northern [[Baja California]].

It grows at elevations of {{Convert|50-2900|m|abbr=on}}.

==Ecology==
At lower elevations, associated trees include oaks and [[ponderosa pine]].<ref name=":02" /> [[Giant sequoia]] bears similarities to the species, but has sharp leaves. In the south–southwest U.S. some have confused bushy [[juniper]]s for incense cedar.<ref name=":02" />

With its thick basal bark,<ref name=":02" /> the incense cedar is one of the most fire- and drought-tolerant plants in California. Although the tree is killed by hot, stand-replacing crown fire, it spreads rapidly after lower-intensity burns.<ref>Franklin, Janet; Spears-Lebrun, Linnea A.; Deutschman, Douglas H.; Marsden, Kim. 2006. Impact of a high-intensity fire on mixed evergreen and mixed conifer forests in the Peninsular Ranges of southern California, USA. Forest Ecology and Management. 235(1-3): 18-29. [65016]</ref> This has given the incense cedar a competitive advantage over other species such as the [[bigcone Douglas-fir]] in recent years. Incense cedar is more [[shade tolerant]] than [[Douglas-fir]], but not as much so as [[Abies grandis|grand]] or [[white fir]]. It grows slowly when needed to outlast competition.<ref name=":02" />

This tree is the preferred host of a [[wood wasp]], ''[[Syntexis libocedrii]]'' a species which lays its eggs in the smoldering wood immediately after a forest fire.<ref name="usfs" /> The tree is also host to incense-cedar mistletoe (''[[Phoradendron libocedri]]''), a [[parasitic plant]] which can often be found hanging from its branches.<ref>{{Jepson Manual|id=7836,7852,7856|taxon=Phoradendron libocedri|first1=Frank G.|last1=Hawksworth|first2=Delbert|last2=Wiens}}</ref> Fire scars provide an entry point for ''Tyromyces amarus'' (pocket dry rot).<ref name=":02" /> ''[[Gymnosporangium]]'' rust disease afflicts the trees, but is rarely fatal.<ref name=":02" />

For numerous birds during the wintertime, ''Calocedrus decurrens'' has been seen to be used for [[foraging]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Morrison |first1=Michael L. |last2=Dahlsten |first2=Donald L. |last3=Tait |first3=Susan M. |last4=Heald |first4=Robert C. |last5=Milne |first5=Kathleen A. |last6=Rowney |first6=David L. |date=1989 |title=Bird foraging on incense-cedar and incense-cedar scale during winter in California |journal=Res. Pap. PSW-Rp-195. Albany, Ca: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Pacific Southwest Research Station. 16 P |volume=195 |url=https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/29116 |language=en |location=Berkeley, CA |pages=PSW–RP–195 |doi=10.2737/psw-rp-195|hdl=2027/umn.31951d028890389 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> According to the [[United States Department of Agriculture]], in areas of the Western Sierra Nevada in California, numerous species of birds are thought to use the incense cedar as a "foraging substrate" so that they can attain as much food as needed.<ref name=":2" /> Human impacts on these trees due to forest management practices have caused issues for many of these birds, threatening the use of the incense cedar as a forage substrate.<ref name=":2" />

==Uses==
The wood is soft and light, and has a pleasant odor and is generally resistant to rot. It has been used for external house siding, interior paneling, and to make moth-resistant [[hope chest]]s.<ref name=":02" /> It was once the primary material for wooden [[pencil]]s, because it is soft and tends to sharpen easily without forming splinters.<ref name=":02" />

===Native Americans===
[[Indigenous peoples of California]] use the plant in traditional medicine,{{how|date=July 2016}} [[basket making]], [[bow and arrow|hunting bows]], building materials, and to produce fire by friction.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20130729054400/http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Calocedrus+decurrens University of Michigan—Dearborn: Native American Ethnobotany of ''Calocedrus decurrens'']</ref> A Northern California tribe used branchlets to filter out sand from water when leaching toxins from acorn meal; foliage also served as a flavoring.<ref name=":02" />

The [[Maidu]] [[Maidu#Local divisions|Concow tribe]] name for the plant is '''hö'-tä''' ([[Konkow language]]).<ref>{{cite book|last1=Chesnut | first1 =Victor King | author1-link=Victor King Chesnut |title=Plants used by the Indians of Mendocino County, California|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vLkUAAAAYAAJ|access-date=24 August 2012|year=1902|publisher=[[United States Government Printing Office|Government Printing Office]]|page = 404}}</ref>

===Cultivation===
''Calocedrus decurrens'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental tree]], for planting in gardens and parks. It is used in traditional, [[xeriscape|xeriscapic]], [[native plant]], and [[wildlife garden]]s; and also in designed [[natural landscaping]] and [[habitat restoration]] projects in California. It is valued for its columnar form and evergreen foliage textures.

The tree is also grown in gardens and parks in cool summer climates, including the [[Pacific Northwest]] in the [[Northwestern United States]] and [[British Columbia]], eastern Great Britain and continental [[Northern Europe]]. In these areas it can develop an especially narrow columnar crown, an unexplained consequence of the cooler climatic conditions that is rare in trees within its warm summer natural range in the [[California Floristic Province]]. Other cultivated species from the family [[Cupressaceae]] can have similar crown forms.<ref name=afm>Mitchell, A. F. (1996). ''Alan Mitchell's Trees of Britain''. Collins {{ISBN|0-00-219972-6}}.</ref>

====Award of Garden Merit====
This plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]],<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/2763/Calocedrus-decurrens/Details | title = ''Calocedrus decurrens'' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 12 April 2020}}</ref> and has the cultivar 'Berrima Gold'.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/67442/Calocedrus-decurrens-Berrima-Gold/Details | title = ''Calocedrus decurrens'' 'Berrima Gold' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 12 April 2020}}</ref>

===Essential oils===
Various species in the family Cupressaceae can be utilized for the creation of [[essential oil]]s.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Ibrahim|first1=Taghreed A.|last2=El-Hefnawy|first2=Hala M.|last3=El-Hela|first3=Atef A.|date=2010-10-10|title=Antioxidant potential and phenolic acid content of certain cucurbitaceous plants cultivated in Egypt|journal=Natural Product Research|volume=24|issue=16|pages=1537–1545|doi=10.1080/14786419.2010.489049|pmid=20835955 |s2cid=42694118 |issn=1478-6419}}</ref> Scientific studies have shown that these essential oils have "strong antimicrobial properties."<ref name=":1"/> Antimicrobial properties are those properties of a substance that lower the levels of microbes, such as [[bacteria]] and [[virus]]es. These antimicrobial properties could potentially be used for therapies in developing countries, although more testing and [[clinical trial]]s should be done before such measures are implemented.<ref name=":1"/>
